procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 12.05.2015 of the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur in DBCRA Nos. 872 and 1066 of 2011.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur issued a Judgment and Order in DBCRA Nos. 872 and 1066 of 2011 on 12.05.2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Doongar Singh & Ors. appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, finding no infirmity in the orders of the court below that would warrant interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India. The Supreme Court was approached because the appellants believed the High Court's order was flawed.

directions: The trial courts must carry out the mandate of Section 309 of the Cr.P.C. as reiterated in judgments of this Court, inter alia, in State of U.P. versus Shambhu Nath Singh and Others, Mohd. Khalid versus State of W.B. and Vinod Kumar versus State of Punjab.

issue.issue_text: Whether the orders of the lower courts suffer from any infirmity that would warrant interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.

facts: The Supreme Court heard the arguments from the counsel for the parties at great length.
The Court also perused the record of the case.
law: The Supreme Court has the power to interfere with the orders of lower courts under Article 136 of the Constitution of India if there is an infirmity in those orders.
application: After hearing the parties and reviewing the record, the Court evaluated the orders of the lower courts to determine if any such infirmity existed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the orders of the lower courts that would warrant its interference under Article 136. Therefore, the Court dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court's practice of granting frequent adjournments and deferring cross-examination without recording special reasons is in accordance with the mandate of the law.

facts: The trial court granted frequent adjournments simply upon being asked.
The cross-examination of witnesses was deferred for long periods of time.
The court failed to record any special reasons for these adjournments and deferrals.
In one instance, after the examination-in-chief of a star witness in a murder case, the matter was adjourned for about four months.
law: Section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) mandates that once a trial commences, it must continue from day to day until all witnesses in attendance have been examined.
A court can only deviate from this day-to-day procedure for "special reasons," which must be recorded in writing.
If witnesses are present in court, the court is required to examine them; adjournment is forbidden in that situation.
The inconvenience of an advocate is not considered a "special reason" to grant an adjournment.
application: The Supreme Court found that the trial court's actions were a direct violation of the mandate of Section 309 Cr.P.C.

The Court expressed its distress, noting that it is a common practice for trial courts to flout this command with impunity, granting adjournments on "flippant grounds" or for the convenience of advocates.
It observed that the trial judge in this case seemed to have completely disregarded the gravity and sanctity of a criminal trial.

The Court warned that such unnecessary adjournments and long deferrals of cross-examination give the accused an opportunity to influence or "get over the witnesses," thereby jeopardizing the administration of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the trial court's practice, holding that granting frequent adjournments and deferring cross-examination without recording special reasons is contrary to the clear and mandatory provisions of Section 309 of the Cr.P.C., which requires trials to be conducted on a continuous, day-to-day basis to ensure a fair and expeditious conclusion.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the orders of the lower courts suffer from any infirmity that would warrant interference by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the orders of the lower courts contained legal and/or factual infirmities that justified the Supreme Court's intervention under Article 136 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the orders of the lower courts were legally sound and did not suffer from any infirmity that would call for the Supreme Court's interference.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court's practice of granting frequent adjournments and deferring cross-examination without recording special reasons is in accordance with the mandate of the law.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that the trial court's practice of granting frequent adjournments, often for the convenience of counsel, violated the mandate of Section 309 of the Cr.P.C. and constituted a serious procedural flaw that vitiated the trial.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that while adjournments may have occurred, they did not cause a miscarriage of justice or constitute an infirmity sufficient to warrant overturning the lower court's decision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inconvenience of an advocate does not constitute a 'special reason' to grant an adjournment and bypass the mandate of Section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: A criminal trial has its own gravity and sanctity.
It is necessary in the interest of justice that eyewitnesses are examined by the prosecution at the earliest.
Once a trial begins, it should invariably proceed from day to day as one method of complying with the law.
The High Court can monitor, supervise, and give directions on the administration side regarding measures to conform to the legislative insistence contained in Section 309 of the Code.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the Court found no substantive legal or factual infirmity in the lower courts' orders that would justify interference with the conviction under Article 136 of the Constitution, it found that the trial was conducted in a manner that "shocks the judicial conscience." The trial court's practice of granting frequent adjournments on mere asking and deferring cross-examination without recording any special reasons was a flagrant violation of the mandatory provisions of Section 309 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
legal_tests_applied: The test for adjournment under Section 309 of the Cr.P.C.: Once examination of a witness has started, the court must continue the trial from day to day until all witnesses in attendance have been examined, and can only deviate from this course by recording reasons.

The jurisdictional requirement for adjournment: Only if there are 'special reasons', which reasons should find a place in the order for adjournment, that alone can confer jurisdiction on the court to adjourn the case.
The definition of a 'special reason': The inconvenience of an advocate is not a 'special reason' for bypassing the mandate of Section 309 of the Code.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate any substantive 'infirmity in the orders of the court below calling for our interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.'

Although the Court agreed that the trial court committed serious procedural violations regarding adjournments, these violations were not deemed sufficient to overturn the conviction on the merits of the case.
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded because the Supreme Court, after a full review, found no legal or factual error in the final orders of the lower courts that would warrant overturning the conviction.
policy_considerations: The Court expressed its anguish and distress that it is an 'almost a common practice and regular occurrence that trial courts flout the said command [of Section 309] with impunity.'

The Court emphasized that 'it is the primary and paramount duty of the criminal courts to ensure that the risk to fair trial is removed and trials are allowed to proceed smoothly without any interruption or obstruction.'
The Court noted that the legislature has 'frowned at granting adjournments' merely to suit the convenience of an advocate.
The Court reiterated that it is 'necessary in the interest of justice that the eye-witnesses are examined by the prosecution at the earliest.'
